content.description: Biology: Cambridge International A Level > Biological Molecules

resources.title: Water Structure & Function

content.topicNotes: Function of Water Water makes up 60-70% of the human body. Life also evolved in a watery environment. Water's chemical structure gives it properties that are vital for life. Uses of water Water is one of the most useful molecules for life. Water acts as a reactant in cells, for example in photosynthesis and hydrolysis reactions. Water provides structural support in cells, for example by keeping them turgid. Water helps keep organisms cool, maintaining body temperature. Hydrogen bonding in water Water molecules are polar, with a slightly negative oxygen atom and slightly positive hydrogen atoms. A polar molecule has an unequal spread of charge. The charges allow water molecules to form hydrogen bonds with each other. Hydrogen bonding gives water properties that are vital for life. Cohesion and adhesion Hydrogen bonds cause cohesion in water. Cohesion is a pull between water molecules. Cohesion pulls water up through xylem vessels in plants. Water also shows adhesion, a pull between water and other polar surfaces. Adhesion helps water stick to the walls of xylem vessels. Thermal properties Water has a high specific heat capacity. A high specific heat capacity means water needs lots of energy to warm up. High specific heat capacity keeps aquatic habitats at a stable temperature. Water has a high latent heat of vaporisation. Evaporation of sweat cools the body down. Water as a solvent Water is a good solvent. Water's polarity attracts charged and polar substances. Hydrophilic substances are polar or ionic and dissolve easily in water. Hydrophobic substances are non-polar and do not dissolve in water. Water carries dissolved substances around the body. Density of water Ice is less dense than liquid water. Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules further apart in ice than in liquid water. Lower density means ice floats on top of liquid water. Floating ice insulates the water below, protecting aquatic organisms from freezing. The Structure of Water The structure of a water molecule helps us to understand hydrogen bonding and the function of water. Contents of a water molecule Water molecules (H2O) are made from: One oxygen atom. Two hydrogen atoms. Polarity Water is a polar molecule. The oxygen atoms in water are slightly negatively charged. The hydrogen atoms in water are slightly positively charged. Hydrogen bonding The polarity of water molecules means that a hydrogen atom on one water molecule is attracted to the oxygen atom on another water molecule. This attraction is called hydrogen bonding. Useful Properties of Water Water is a major component of cells and is essential to life as we know it (60–70% of the human body is made up of water). The properties of water that make it such a useful substance are: High latent heat of vaporisation The latent heat of vaporisation is the amount of energy needed to change one gram of a liquid substance to a gas. As liquid water heats up, hydrogen bonding makes it difficult to separate the water molecules from each other. This means that a lot of energy is needed for water to evaporate. When water evaporates, energy is used up - this cools the environment where the evaporation is taking place. This is why sweating helps with body temperature regulation. High heat capacity Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat one kilogram of a substance must absorb or lose to change its temperature by 1oC. Water has a high heat capacity so takes a long time to heat and cool. The specific heat capacity of water is much larger than sand. This is why land cools faster than the sea. Water is used by warm blooded animals to more evenly disperse heat in their bodies. Good solvent Water is a good solvent because ions and polar molecules can easily dissolve in it. Water is a polar molecule. This means that the positive end of the water molecule attracts negative ions and the negative end will attract positive ions. Good metabolite Water is used or formed in many metabolic reactions, such as condensation and hydrolysis reactions. ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi + energyA bond is broken and a water molecule is used up and so this is a hydrolysis reaction. ADP + Pi + energy → ATP + H2OA new bond is formed and a water molecule is released and so this is a condensation reaction. Cohesive properties The strong attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonds is called cohesion. Cohesion produces surface tension where water meets air. This is why water forms droplets when placed on a dry surface rather than being flattened out by gravity. Plants use this natural phenomenon to help transport water from their roots to their leaves.

resources.title: Xylem

content.topicNotes: Structure The xylem are plant vessels that are responsible for transporting water and mineral ions. The structure of the xylem is specialised for this role. Vessel elements The xylem vessels are long, tubes of cells that run up the stem of plants. The cells of the xylem are called vessel elements. The vessel elements in the xylem are dead. End walls The vessel elements are stacked on top one another. There are no cell walls at the ends of each vessel element. This creates a continuous tube for water to flow through. Lignin The walls of the xylem are lined with a waterproof polymer called lignin. Lignin reinforces the walls of the vessel elements to provide structural support. Cohesion-Tension Theory Water and inorganic ions travel up the xylem through cohesion and tension. The steps involved in this process are: Transpiration Some of the water in the leaves is used in photosynthesis. Most of the water in the leaves evaporates in a process called transpiration. Tension The loss of water from the leaves creates tension in the xylem. Tension is the formation of hydrogen bonds between water molecules and the sides of the xylem vessel elements. Water in the xylem is pulled upwards by this tension towards the leaves. Cohesion Individual water molecules also form hydrogen bonds with each other. This process is called cohesion. When water molecules are pulled up the xylem, other molecules of water are also pulled upwards due to cohesion. The combination of cohesion and tension together continuously pull water upwards to replace water that has been lost in the leaves by transpiration. Diffusion in the roots When water is pulled up the stem, the water potential at the bottom of the plant decreases. Water diffuses into the roots via osmosis down its water potential gradient. Water in the roots travels via the apoplast or symplast pathway into the xylem. In the apoplastic pathway, water moves through the cell walls of adjacent root cells. In the symplastic pathway, water moves through the cytoplasm & vacuoles of adjacent root cells via the plasmodesmata. The Casparian strip Near the root xylem vessels, there is an impermeable strip in the cell walls of root cells. This is called the Capsarian strip. The Casparian strip blocks the apoplast pathway as water can't pass through the strip. This means water must pass through the cytoplasm to continue into the xylem. Cohesion-Tension Theory The two processes that allow water to travel up the xylem are cohesion and tension. Cohesion Cohesion is the formation of hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Water is pulled up the xylem by other water molecules. Tension Tension is the formation of hydrogen bonds between water molecules and the vessel elements walls. Water is pulled up the xylem by tension in the leaves.

resources.title: Zoos, Seedbanks, & Other Conservation Methods

content.topicNotes: Methods Used by Zoos Zoos are key to ex situ conservation efforts. They play a role in scientific research, reintroductions, education, and conservation of genetic diversity. Ex situ conservation Conservation ex situ means that organisms that need conserving are moved out of their habitat and protected elsewhere. Zoos and seed banks both play a role in ex situ conservation. Ex situ conservation removes the organisms under threat from those threats, but sampled individuals from an environment will always have a lower genetic diversity than the original population. Zoos try and conserve genetic diversity of animals and increase awareness of the importance of conservation. Education Zoos play a vital role in education. Visitors to the zoo receive information about the importance of conserving vulnerable species. Many zoos have the opportunity for schools to visit, where children will be taught why conservation is important in an engaging and interactive way. -Some zoos will also run outreach programmes, where they visit schools to talk more about the work that they do. Zoos also conduct a lot of scientific research. This includes genetic research & animal behaviour research. Reintroduction programmes Zoos try to reintroduce animals into the wild where it is possible. An example of a successful reintroduction programme is the reintroduction of the golden lion tamarin to Brazil. It was a collaborative effort with more than 40 zoos in several countries. Reintroduction programmes can be difficult if the animal has lived in the zoo its whole life and would be unable to survive in the world. This is true of most big cats who never learnt how to hunt properly. Captive breeding programmes Zoos run captive breeding programmes to increase numbers of individuals in an endangered species. Genetic diversity is a key consideration for captive breeding programmes. By comparing genomes of the captive animals, zoos can work together to match up individuals which would produce genetically diverse offspring. Success of captive breeding Captive breeding programmes have varying levels of success. An example of a successful programme is the panda in China. Captive breeding has been used in combination with reintroduction programmes, resulting in the panda no longer being endangered. Some captive breeding programmes have lower levels of success because zoos cannot recreate the conditions that are needed. Frozen zoos Some zoos freeze the sperm, eggs, or embryos of captive animals to form "frozen zoos". These can be useful as sperm can be taken from males after death. This means their sperm can still be used for artificial insemination. Freezing the genetic material allows it to be stored for longer and used in future assisted reproduction methods (e.g. IVF). Conservation of Plants Seed banks play an important role in ex situ conservation. They can store seeds to conserve genetic diversity. Botanical gardens house many plant species and often have seed banks. Storing seeds Storing seeds is an important way to conserve genetic diversity of plants. Many seeds are happy to be dried and frozen, and will survive in dormancy like this for hundreds of years. For other plants, storage has proven more difficult because the seeds are not amenable to normal storage methods, or, if they are mosses and ferns, they do not have seeds. Conserving genetic diversity To ensure that a sufficient level of genetic diversity is captured, it is important to store seeds from different populations and areas. Seed banks have limited space. It is important that the most relevant seed types are collected to ensure the maximum genetic diversity is stored. Having a genetically diverse collection is important because some of the plants may have properties which would be beneficial. For example, there may be a strain of wheat which is particularly resistant to drought, or to flooding. Role of seed banks Seed banks exist to conserve as many species as possible, capturing the most genetic diversity they can, but they also serve other purposes. Seed banks are used for research by botanic gardens, as well as for raising awareness of the importance of conserving plants. Kew Gardens runs the Millennium Seed Bank project, which has the largest, most diverse collection of seeds in the world. Botanical gardens Botanical gardens are important for the conservation and study of plant species. Many botanical gardens also house seed banks. Conserved areas & national parks Conserved areas like national parks are also important for preserving biodiversity. National parks are large areas of land containing numerous plant and animal species. Such areas are protected from development. This helps protect the native species that live there. Conserved areas of water and marine ecosystems are called marine parks. They have a similar function to national parks.

resources.title: lac Operon

content.topicNotes: Transcriptional Level Regulation of gene expression in prokaryotic and sometimes eukaryotic cells occurs at the transcriptional level. Simply, if a cell does not transcribe DNA into mRNA, protein synthesis does not occur. Operons Bacterial genes are often organized into common pathways called operons, for more coordinated regulation of expression. All the genes in one operon are transcribed as a long, single piece of mRNA. The operon includes a regulatory gene that codes for a repressor protein which binds to the operator, preventing RNA polymerase from transcribing the gene of interest. Regulatory molecules In prokaryotic cells, there are three types of regulatory molecules that can affect the expression of operons: Repressors are proteins which suppress transcription of a gene in response to an external stimulus. Activators are proteins which increase transcription of a gene in response to an external stimulus. Inducers are small molecules which activate or repress transcription depending on the needs of the cell and substrate availability. Lac operon The lac operon is an inducible operon which contains the genes necessary to acquire and process lactose from the environment. This is useful for E. coli bacteria because it means it can use lactose as an energy resource when glucose concentrations are low. Lac operon When glucose is absent and lactose is present, the catabolite activator protein (CAP) binds to the operator sequence to activate transcription. If lactose is absent, the repressor binds to the operator to prevent transcription. Lac operon is only transcribed when glucose is low AND lactose is present. Comparison to eukaryotes Transcription factors are involved in the regulation of gene expression in eukaryotes at the transcriptional level. Eukaryote genes are NOT organized into operons. However, one transcription factor may regulate a group of genes involved in a particular function.

resources.title: t-Tests

content.topicNotes: Hypothesis Testing A hypothesis is an assumption made about the value of a particular parameter. We can use a $$t$$-test to determine whether the difference between the means of two populations are statistically significant. Null and alternative hypotheses The null hypothesis, $$H_0$$, is a hypothesis that is assumed to be correct. In a $$t$$-test, the null hypothesis is that there is no significant difference between the two population means. The alternative hypothesis, $$H_1$$ is that there is a significant difference between the two population means. A decision is then made as to whether or not there is sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. $$p$$-value In order to test a hypothesis, we consider how likely the hypothesis is to be true. The probability of the null hypothesis being true is referred to as the $$p$$-value. Significance level If the probability of the null hypothesis being true is less likely than a given "significance level", we reject the null hypothesis. The significance level used in biology is often 5%. Test statistic The test statistic used to calculate $$p$$-values is equal to: $$t = \frac{\large\overline{x}_1-\overline{x}_2}{\large \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}$$ $$\overline{x}_1$$ = is the mean of sample one. $$\overline{x}_2$$ = is the mean of sample two. $$s_1$$ is the standard deviation of sample one. $$s_2$$ is the standard deviation of sample two. $$n_1$$ is the number of measures in sample one. $$n_1$$ is the number of measures in sample two. Degrees of freedom The degrees of freedom is equal to $$n_1+n_2-2$$. Determine the critical value Once you have determined the value of the test statistic, you need to use a statistics table to determine the critical value. The critical value will be the value at the significance level (5%) of your particular degrees of freedom. If the calculated value is greater than the critical value, you reject the null hypothesis. If the calculated value is less than the critical value, you accept the null hypothesis.

resources.title: Describe how directional selection leads to evolution in a population using an example.

content.questionTitleMd: Describe how directional selection leads to evolution in a population using an example.
content.markScheme:
**Directional selection** is a type of natural selection that favours traits in a particular direction, leading to evolution in a population. (1)
**How it leads to evolution:** Directional selection leads to the evolution of new traits and adaptations (1) that help organisms better survive and reproduce in changing environments, this results in the divergence of populations into new species. (1)
**Example:** In a population of finches, beaks that are better adapted to cracking hard seeds are favoured, leading to an increase in beak size over time. (1)

resources.title: Describe how disruptive selection leads to speciation in a population using an example.
resources.topicPath: Biology: AQA A Level > Genetics & Ecosystems (A2 only) > Evolution > Types of Selection > Biology: Cambridge International A Level > Selection & Evolution (A2 Only) > Natural & Artificial Selection > Types of Selection > Biology: Edexcel A A Level > On the Wild Side > Evolution > Causes of Speciation > Biology: OCR A A Level > Genetics, Evolution & Ecosystems > Patterns of Inheritance > Speciation

content.questionTitleMd: Describe how disruptive selection leads to speciation in a population using an example.
content.markScheme:
**Disruptive selection** is a type of natural selection that occurs when two or more extreme traits are favoured over intermediate traits, leading to the formation of two or more distinct phenotypes. (1)
**How it leads to speciation:** Disruptive selection can lead to speciation where the two distinct phenotypes become reproductively isolated from each other, resulting in the formation of two separate species over time. (1)
Any ONE **examples** of: - In a population of fish, individuals with either long or short fins are favoured over those with intermediate-length fins, causing the population to split into two distinct phenotypes (1) - *Any other reasonable example* (1)

resources.title: Describe how each type of selection could lead to evolutionary change in populations.

content.questionTitleMd: Describe how each type of selection could lead to evolutionary change in populations.
content.markScheme:
**Stabilising selection**: could lead to evolutionary change by reducing the variance in a trait, thereby making the population more homogeneous. (1)
**Divergent selection**: could lead to evolutionary change by promoting the development of new and distinct forms in different environments. (1)
**Directional selection**: could lead to evolutionary change by altering the mean value of a trait in a population, thereby shifting the distribution of the trait over time. (1)
**Disruptive selection**: could lead to evolutionary change by increasing variation within a population, allowing for the development of new and distinct forms that are better adapted to different environments. (1)

content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Limiting factors are those factors that directly affect the rate of photosynthesis by restricting the availability of reactants or creating unfavorable conditions.
A decrease in the availability of light, carbon dioxide, or water can slow down the rate of photosynthesis as these reactants are essential for the process to occur. High temperatures can also decrease the rate of photosynthesis by denaturing enzymes involved in the process.

**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
The Hardy-Weinberg Principle is a theoretical model that predicts the frequency of alleles in a population based on genetic equilibrium. The Hardy-Weinberg Principle predicts that the frequency of alleles in a population will remain constant from generation to generation. Unless acted upon by other factors such as mutation, selection, migration, or genetic drift. For the Hardy-Weinberg Principle to hold, five conditions must be met: a large population size, no mutation, no migration, no selection, and random mating.

content.markScheme:
1. Decide which level you think the answer is first. 2. Then read the answer again. 3. Think about what the answer has done well and what can be improved. 4. Decide on a mark. **Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
**Description:**
The Mark and Recapture method involves capturing a sample of individuals from a population, marking them, releasing them back into the population, and then capturing another sample of individuals and counting the number of marked individuals in the second sample. The ratio of marked individuals in the second sample to the total number of individuals captured in the second sample can be used to estimate the ratio of marked individuals in the entire population, allowing for estimation of the total population size.
**Explanation:**
The method assumes that the marking process does not affect the behavior or survival of the individuals, and that the population is closed, with no migration or change in size between the two sampling periods. Errors can arise from incorrect assumptions about the population, such as unequal capture probabilities between marked and unmarked individuals, or changes in the population size during the period between the two samples.

content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Meiosis is a type of cell division that produces four genetically diverse haploid cells from a single diploid cell. Meiosis involves two rounds of cell division, known as meiosis I and meiosis II, each consisting of prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase stages.
During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments of DNA in a process known as crossing over. The homologous chromosomes then separate and move to opposite poles of the cell, resulting in two haploid cells with sister chromatids still connected.
During meiosis II, the sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles of the cell, resulting in four haploid cells, each with a unique combination of alleles.

content.markScheme:
- **Recombination** is the process by which <mark>genetic material from different chromosomes</mark> is <mark>shuffled to form a new combination of genes</mark> (1)
- **How separates linked genes:** Recombination leads to the separation of linked genes as it shuffles the genetic material from different chromosomes, leading to <mark>new combinations of genes that are not linked</mark> (1)
- **Independent assortment** refers to <mark>the random distribution of chromosomes during meiosis</mark>, which leads to <mark>a shuffling of genetic material</mark> and can result in the separation of linked genes (1)
- **Crossing over** is another <mark>mechanism of recombination</mark> that involves <mark>the exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes during meiosis</mark>, leading to the separation of linked genes (1)

**Indicative content**
The process of speciation is the divergence of a single species into two or more distinct species. Speciation can occur through several mechanisms including allopatric speciation, where a geographic barrier separates populations and prevents gene flow, and sympatric speciation, where populations of a species diverge despite overlapping geographic ranges. Speciation is significant in evolution as it can lead to the formation of new species over time, increasing biodiversity and allowing for the adaptation to new environments.

**Indicative content**
Transcription involves the separation of the two strands of DNA, with one strand serving as a template for the synthesis of complementary RNA bases.
RNA polymerase is the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of the phosphodiester bonds between the RNA nucleotides, using the template strand as a guide.
Transcription proceeds in the 5' to 3' direction, resulting in the synthesis of a single-stranded RNA molecule that is complementary to the template DNA strand.
The newly synthesized RNA molecule can be further processed, including the addition of a 5' cap and a poly-A tail, before leaving the nucleus to undergo a translation into a protein.

Variation refers to differences between individuals in a population. **Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
DNA is a double-stranded helix made up of nucleotides.
Each nucleotide consists of a sugar molecule, a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base.
The nitrogenous bases are adenine, thymine, guanine, and cytosine, and they pair with each other through hydrogen bonds: adenine pairs with thymine, and guanine pairs with cytosine.
The sugar and phosphate molecules form the backbone of the DNA molecule, while the nitrogenous bases are found in the middle and are held together by hydrogen bonds.

content.questionTitleMd: Explain the concept of multiple alleles and provide an example to illustrate their inheritance in a population.
content.markScheme:
1. Decide which level you think the answer is first. 2. Then read the answer again. 3. Think about what the answer has done well and what can be improved. 4. Decide on a mark. **Level 3 (5 marks):** The answer is well organised and ties together relevant features to provide an explanation on their combined impact and the related context.
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Multiple alleles refer to a trait that is controlled by three or more alleles at a single locus. An example of a trait with multiple alleles is ABO blood type, which is determined by the presence of A, B, or O alleles.
Inheritance of multiple alleles occurs through the principles of Mendelian inheritance, where offspring receive one allele from each parent. The presence of multiple alleles can affect the phenotype frequency in a population.
The concept of codominance or incomplete dominance can also come into play, as seen in the case of ABO blood type where the presence of both A and B alleles result in AB blood type, which is a combination of both A and B phenotypes.

Our bodies have specialized cells called receptors that can detect dangerous stimuli. When these receptors detect a threat, they send electrical impulses to the sensory neuron, which then relays the signal to the motor neuron via the relay neuron. content.markScheme:

**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Inheritance refers to the passing on of genetic traits from parent to offspring through the transmission of genetic information. Dominant alleles are traits that will always be expressed if present in an individual, while recessive alleles are only expressed when two copies are present. Chromosomes carry genes, the basic units of heredity, which are responsible for determining an organism's traits. During reproduction, chromosomes are passed from parent to offspring, ensuring the transmission of genetic information from one generation to the next. The transmission of genetic information from one generation to the next ensures that traits are passed down from parents to their offspring, allowing for the continuation of the species.

**Indicative content**
Gills are thin filaments which are highly branched and folded, this creates a large surface area. Gills also contain lamellae, to further increase the surface area close to the large bloodstream. content.questionTitleMd: Explain why linkage sometimes leads to genes being inherited together by describing linkage and explain how recombination leads to the separation of linked genes, including a description of independent assortment and crossing over.
content.markScheme:
- **Linkage** refers to <mark>the tendency for certain genes to be inherited together</mark> on the <mark>same chromosome</mark>. (1) Linked genes are <mark>genes that are located on the same chromosome</mark> and tend to be <mark>inherited together</mark>. (1)

resources.topicPath: Biology: Cambridge International A Level > Selection & Evolution (A2 Only) > Evolution > Evolution by Natural Selection

content.questionTitleMd: Explain why natural selection leads to evolution.
content.markScheme:
1. Decide which level you think the answer is first. 2. Then read the answer again. 3. Think about what the answer has done well and what can be improved. 4. Decide on a mark. **Level 3 (5 marks):** The answer is well organised and ties together the process of natural selection and its role in evolution in detail.
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer describes the overall process of natural selection.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant description of natural selection.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Natural selection is the process by which certain traits become more or less common in a population over time due to differences in reproductive success. The process of natural selection involves three key elements: variation in traits among individuals, the heritability of those traits, and differential reproductive success. Individuals with traits that are better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing their advantageous traits on to their offspring. Over time, the frequency of these advantageous traits increases in the population.
Natural selection is the main mechanism of evolution, leading to the development of new species and the adaptation of species to their environment over time.

content.questionTitleMd: Explain why selection can lead to deviation from the Hardy-Weinberg Principle.
content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer is well organised and ties together the concepts of selection and provides an explanation of how selection can lead to deviation from the Hardy-Weinberg Principle.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant concepts of selection.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Selection occurs when certain alleles or genotypes confer an advantage or disadvantage to individuals in a population, leading to differences in reproductive success. Over time, the frequency of alleles or genotypes that confer a fitness advantage will increase in the population, while the frequency of those that confer a fitness disadvantage will decrease, this results in the deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
Selection is a fundamental mechanism of evolution, shaping the composition of populations over time and leading to the development of new traits and the evolution of new species. Selection acts on the frequency of alleles or genotypes in populations, either increasing or decreasing the frequency of specific alleles or genotypes over time and leading to deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

**Stabilising and divergent:** Stabilising by reducing variation, maintaining status quo, while divergent which increases variation, leads to new forms. (1)
**Stabilising and directional:** Stabilising by reducing variation, maintaining status quo, while directional which increases variation by changing the mean of a trait. (1)
**Divergent and directional:** Divergent by increasing variation through differences in the environment, while directional which increases variation by selecting for an extreme. (1)
**Directional and disruptive:** Directional which changes the mean of a trait, while disruptive which increases variation by favouring both extremes. (1)

content.questionTitleMd: Explain why the inheritance patterns of dominant and recessive traits are different, providing examples of each and explaining how these patterns impact the phenotype of an organism.
content.markScheme:
- **Dominant traits** are expressed when just <mark>one copy of the dominant allele is present</mark> (1)
- **Recessive traits** are only expressed when <mark>two copies of the recessive allele are present</mark> (1)
- **Dominant trait example:** The brown eye colour. It is expressed even if an individual <mark>has just one dominant allele</mark> for brown eyes (1)
- **Recessive trait example:** The blue eye colour. It is only expressed when an individual has <mark>two copies of the recessive allele</mark> for blue eyes (1)
- The traits **impact the phenotype** of an organism by <mark>determining which traits are expressed and which are hidden</mark> (1)

resources.topicPath: Biology: Cambridge International A Level > Transport in Mammals > Transport of Oxygen & Carbon Dioxide > Oxygen Dissociation

content.questionTitleMd: Explain why the partial pressure of oxygen influences the percentage saturation of haemoglobin.
content.markScheme:
1. Decide which level you think the answer is first. 2. Then read the answer again. 3. Think about what the answer has done well and what can be improved. 4. Decide on a mark. **Level 3 (5 marks):** The answer is well organised and ties together relevant features to provide an explanation on their combined impact and the related context.
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
When the partial pressure of oxygen increases, the percentage saturation of haemoglobin increases. This means that the first oxygen molecule will bind to haemoglobin, which will cause a conformational change in haemoglobin polypeptide. This increases oxygen molecules to bind to the iron ion more easily. Once more molecules of oxygen bind, it becomes difficult for more oxygen molecules to bind as the iron ions are already occupied.

**Indicative content**
Glycogen is a polysaccharide made from many alpha glucose molecules. content.questionTitleMd: Haemoglobin is one of the most important proteins in the body. It reacts within different concentrations of gases to determine its affinity towards oxygen. Outline how different concentrations allow haemoglobin to perform its job.
content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Haemoglobin needs to have a high affinity to oxygen in areas of high oxygen concentration. This means that, there will be a strong attraction to holding onto oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin. When red blood cells carrying oxygen arrive at respiring cells or tissue, the low concentration of oxygen causes a low affinity to oxygen. This results in haemoglobin readily dissociating from oxygen, to allow oxygen to diffuse to where it needs to go.

content.questionTitleMd: It is essential that we have different responses to react towards different situations. Compare and contrast the different responses using examples.
content.markScheme:
1. Decide which level you think the answer is first. 2. Then read the answer again. 3. Think about what the answer has done well and what can be improved. 4. Decide on a mark. **Level 3 (5-6 marks):** The answer is well organised and ties together relevant features to provide an explanation on their combined impact and the related context.
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
**Response type 1:**
In life-threatening situations, such as placing your hand near a naked flame, our body initiates an automatic response. When heat is detected by thermoreceptors in the skin, an electrical impulse travels down the sensory neuron to the relay neuron in the spinal cord, bypassing the brain to facilitate a faster response. From there, the impulse travels to the motor neuron, which is connected to an effector, usually a muscle, causing it to contract and move the arm away from the flame.
**Response type 2:**
In less dangerous situations, the stimuli will generate a slower response compared to the automatic response. For instance, when thermoreceptors detect heat from the sun shining down on your arm, an electrical signal travels from the receptors to the sensory neuron, then to the brain and spinal cord, and finally to the motor neuron. This response does not bypass the brain and spinal cord, and instead of activating a muscle, it triggers sweat glands under the skin to release sweat, which cools the body down.

content.questionTitleMd: Jane was investigating which part of a plant was growing faster, the tip of the root or the tip of the shoot. Jane prepared a single microscope slide of each tip to compare. Explain why Jane can use a measurement to form a conclusion by mentioning what Jane could calculate to make this comparison and suggest how Jane could improve the reliability of her conclusion.
content.markScheme:
**Measurement to calculate:** Jane could calculate a mitotic index. (1) Mitotic index is the proportion of cells undergoing mitosis OR divide the number of cells with visible chromosomes by the total number of cells. (1)
**Conclusion from calculation:** Jane could calculate the mitotic index with the same area for each tip (1) and the tip with a greater index would be growing faster. (1)
**Reliability can be improved by:** Jane could repeat with multiple shoot and root tips from the same plant and take a mean to improve the reliability. (1)

**Indicative content**
When we breathe out a doctor can measure the forced expiratory volume.
Forced expiratory volume is the maximum volume a person can expire in one second. This is not the measure of the total volume of gas inside the lungs because there is a small amount of residual air always inside the lungs to prevent the alveoli from closing.

content.questionTitleMd:
Mitochondria DNA is frequently extracted from cells by scientists investigating evolutionary patterns. A sample of skeletal tissue was first placed in an ice-cold buffer solution and then homogenised. The resulting homogenate was then filtered and the mitochondria were extracted from the filtrate by ultracentrifugation. First, the filtrate was spun at 1000g, and the supernatant was removed and spun again at 7000g to extract the mitochondria.

Suggest why skeletal tissue was used and explain the steps used by the scientists to extract the mitochondria.
content.markScheme:
**Why skeletal tissue was used:** Skeletal tissue was used because cells in skeletal tissue has a high concentration of mitochondria. (1)
**Steps:**
Any FOUR of: - Ice cold buffer solution was used to reduce enzyme activity and prevent proteins from denaturing (1) - The solution was homogenised to break plasma membrane and release organelles (1) - The homogenate was filtered to separate cell debris from organelles. (1) - The solution was filtered and spun at 1000g to separate out heavy organelles and to make the nucleus sink to the bottom of the tube to form a pellet (1) - Mitochondria remains in supernatant so the solution was spun at 7000g to form a pellet to separate out mitochondria (1)

**Indicative content**
The circulatory system is responsible for transporting nutrients and gases such as oxygen around the body. Mammals have a double circulatory system, one called the pulmonary circulation and the other called the systemic circulation. Oxygen-carrying blood is called oxygenated blood and it is pumped around the body, whereas deoxygenated blood is pumped to the lungs.

content.questionTitleMd: Outline how changes in DNA can lead to genetic variation.
content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Changes in DNA can occur through mutations, which can be caused by errors in DNA replication, exposure to mutagens, or spontaneous changes. Mutations can lead to changes in the sequence of nucleotides in DNA, which can affect the structure and function of proteins. Changes in protein structure and function can alter the phenotype of an organism, leading to genetic variation. Additionally, changes in DNA can also occur through recombination, which involves the shuffling of genetic material during meiosis.

content.questionTitleMd: Outline how competition and niche differentiation can lead to the formation of two separate species within a single ecosystem.
content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Competition for resources between two individuals of the same species may result in the individuals adapting to use different resources to minimise competition. This niche differentiation can eventually lead to the development of physical or behavioural differences between the individuals. Over time, physical or behavioural differences may become irreversible, leading to the formation of two distinct species. The two species may then coexist in the same ecosystem, each occupying a different niche and avoiding competition for resources.

content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Divergent selection and allopatric speciation is the evolutionary process where individuals in a population diverge into two distinct forms, adapting to different environments. Divergent selection can drive genetic differences between populations, leading to speciation. Allopatric speciation is where geographical isolation leads to speciation. When populations are geographically isolated and subject to different selective pressures, divergent selection can drive the evolution of distinct traits in each population, eventually leading to the formation of two separate species.

Habitat destruction reduces the area available for native species to live in and can cause population declines or extinction. Introduction of non-native species can disrupt food webs, compete with native species, and lead to declines in biodiversity. Conservation efforts can address habitat destruction by protecting and restoring important habitats, such as wetlands, forests, and grasslands. Controlling the introduction and spread of non-native species can also be a key component of conservation efforts, through measures such as quarantine, eradication, and monitoring.

**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Natural selection is the process by which organisms with advantageous traits are more likely to survive and reproduce. As a result, over time, the frequency of these advantageous traits in a population increases while the frequency of disadvantageous traits decreases.
This leads to adaptation, where a population becomes better suited to its environment, as the advantageous traits enable the organisms to better survive and reproduce in that environment. This can lead to the development of new species or subspecies over time.

**Indicative content**
Post-translational modification can affect protein function in various ways, such as altering the stability, activity, localization, or interaction of the protein.
For example, phosphorylation of a protein can change its activity by inducing conformational changes or creating new binding sites for other proteins.
Acetylation can affect the stability of a protein by preventing protein degradation, while ubiquitination can mark a protein for degradation by the proteasome.
Lipid modification can anchor a protein to a membrane or regulate protein activity through interactions with other lipids or proteins.

content.questionTitleMd: Outline how sexual reproduction contributes to genetic diversity.
content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of gametes from two different individuals, which results in the production of offspring with unique combinations of genetic material. The random assortment of homologous chromosomes during meiosis I and the crossing over of genetic material during meiosis II further increase genetic diversity.
Additionally, mutations that occur during DNA replication and recombination events can also contribute to genetic diversity in offspring.
The process of independent assortment during fertilization means that each offspring will inherit a unique combination of genes from their parents, contributing to genetic diversity.

**Indicative content**
**How it occurs:** Mechanisms of speciation include geographic isolation, reproductive isolation, and genetic divergence. Physical barriers such as rivers, mountains, or oceans can separate populations, leading to the development of different adaptations over time. If populations are reproductively isolated, they cannot interbreed and exchange genetic material, leading to the development of distinct genetic lineages.
**Significance in evolution:** Speciation is a key process in the development of biodiversity and the evolution of new species, it allows for the generation of novel adaptations and the development of new ecosystems, leading to the overall diversity of life on Earth.

Plants lose water through a process called transpiration. This creates tension in the xylem formed by hydrogen bonds between water molecules and the sides of the xylem vessel elements. Both osmosis and reverse osmosis occur across a semipermeable membrane. Osmosis is the movement of water from an area of high water potential to an area of low water potential. resources.title: Sugar is produced in leaves however, these products need to be transported to other parts of the plant. Describe how sugar gets transported around the plant.
resources.topicPath: Biology: AQA A Level > Substance Exchange > Mass Transport > Phloem > Biology: Cambridge International A Level > Transport in Plants > Transport in Plants > Phloem

content.questionTitleMd: Sugar is produced in leaves however, these products need to be transported to other parts of the plant. Describe how sugar gets transported around the plant.
content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
Sucrose produced in the source cells is actively transported into companion cells via co-transport with H+ ions via active transport. Sucrose diffuses into the sieve tube element creating a high concentration of sugar, whilst lowering the water potential near the source at the top. This creates a concentration gradient because of a low concentration of sucrose near the bottom of the plant wherewater potential is high. This creates a hydrostatic pressure gradient which allows a mass transport of sucrose from source to sink.

content.markScheme:
1. Decide which level you think the answer is first. 2. Then read the answer again. 3. Think about what the answer has done well and what can be improved. 4. Decide on a mark. **Level 3 (5 marks):** The answer is well organised and ties together relevant features to provide an explanation on their combined impact and the related context.
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.
**Level 0 (0 marks):** No relevant content.

**Indicative content**
In the lungs, there is a high concentration of oxygen (high partial pressure). Therefore, haemoglobin needs to have a high affinity towards oxygen to hold onto it tightly. This increases the chance of forming oxyhaemoglobin.
When the red blood cells carrying oxygen move around the bloodstream, it holds onto the oxygen tightly. When the red blood cells arrive at respiring cells or tissues, there is a low concentration of oxygen (low partial pressure). As a result, the affinity changes and haemoglobin has a low affinity towards oxygen, causing oxygen to readily dissociate from haemoglobin.

content.markScheme:
**Level 2 (3-4 marks):** The answer outlines relevant features and provides explanations on their impact.
**Level 1 (1-2 marks):** The answer outlines some relevant features.

**Indicative content**
DNA replication is semi-conservative because when it occurs the DNA double-strand splits up and each original DNA strand acts as a template. Free nucleotides then join the original strands by moving toward their complementary bases. Two new DNA molecules are produced which are genetically identical. Therefore, each new DNA molecule contains 1 original strand and 1 new strand.

**Indicative content**
**What is expiration:** Expiration is when we breathe out.
**How expiration happens:** As we breathe out our external intercostal muscles and the diaphragm relax, moving upwards. This movement decreases the volume inside the lungs, causing an increase in pressure. The increase in pressure results in a pressure gradient between inside and outside of the lungs. Air is then drawn out of the lungs.

Cancer is uncontrolled cell division. (1)
Vinka alkaloids stop cell division by preventing mitosis / anaphase of mitosis. (1)
